title: MCMC
oneLine: Sample from a distribution you can only evaluate up to a constant, by building a chain whose stationary distribution is it.

paras: Bayesian inference needs the posterior, and the posterior's normalizing constant is an integral that is usually intractable. MCMC sidesteps it: construct a random walk whose long-run visiting frequency IS the posterior, then run it and treat the visited states as samples. Because the acceptance rule uses a RATIO of densities, the unknown constant cancels.

The practical consequence is that you get a completely general inference engine at the cost of correlated samples and a convergence question. Neither is free - a chain can look healthy and still have missed a mode entirely.
Metropolis-Hastings accepts a proposal with probability given by the density ratio, where the intractable constant cancels:
sections.texNote: Only the UNNORMALIZED density p-tilde appears, which is the whole trick.

theta = init
for _ in range(n_steps):
    prop = theta + sigma * np.random.randn()
    # log-space ratio: the normalizing constant is absent by construction
    if np.log(np.random.rand()) < log_post(prop) - log_post(theta):
        theta = prop
    chain.append(theta)

# Validate against a case with a closed form before trusting it anywhere else.

sections.caption: R-hat below 1.01 says the chains agree, not that the model is right - chains started near each other can agree while all missing a mode.

takeaways: The acceptance ratio cancels the normalizing constant, which is why an unnormalized density suffices.
Samples are correlated, so effective sample size matters more than raw draw count - and tail ESS more than bulk.
Convergence diagnostics check the SAMPLER, never the model; posterior predictive checks are what test the model.
